findings.claim: niche marketing defined as “Selling different versions of a similar product to different groups of customers” (the same wrong definition in the <dfn> data-def and in glossary_terms[3])
findings.truth: That describes differentiated marketing. Niche marketing means aiming a product at one small, specific group of customers with shared needs. The lesson’s own prose and flashcard 3 say this correctly, so the definition contradicts the lesson.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1 (mass and niche markets); internal contradiction with the same lesson’s prose and flashcard

findings.claim: “when Topshop stopped appealing to its core 16–25 segment, it collapsed into administration in 2021” (repeated in flashcard 14)
findings.truth: Topshop’s owner Arcadia Group entered administration on 30 November 2020. ASOS bought the Topshop brand out of administration in February 2021 and the shops closed.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Topshop (Arcadia administration 30 Nov 2020; ASOS purchase 1 Feb 2021)

findings.claim: flashcard 8 asks for “a UK brand built on penetration pricing for low-income shoppers” in a lesson about segmentation
findings.truth: Penetration pricing is a launch tactic (low price, later raised). Aldi runs a permanent everyday-low-price model. Lesson 1 teaches income segmentation, not pricing, so the question should ask about the segment.
Ben Francis started Gymshark in his parents’ garage in Bromsgrove, Worcestershire; the company is now based in Solihull. Not mark-affecting, and not re-verified this session.
findings.evidence: general knowledge; not confirmed against a source in this session

findings.claim: “Writing about USP and brand image from a real named business lifts you straight into the top band for 12-mark evaluations.”
findings.truth: An invented mark-scheme rule. Application to a named business is necessary but not sufficient: a 12-mark evaluate answer also needs a two-sided argument and a justified conclusion.
findings.evidence: spec section 4 (assessment objectives: AO2 application plus AO3 analysis and evaluation)

findings.claim: “Cadbury discontinued Wispa for seven years in the 1990s … then relaunched it in 2008”
findings.truth: Wispa was discontinued in 2003 (replaced by Dairy Milk Bubbly), returned as a limited edition in October 2007 and permanently in October 2008 — a five-year gap, not seven, and in the 2000s, not the 1990s.

findings.claim: “This is the most common misconception in the exam” (key fact) and “The top misconception examiners see is confusing market growth with product sales growth” (exam tip)
findings.truth: Fabricated examiner claims. The teaching point is sound; the ranking of it as what examiners see most often is invented and unverifiable.
findings.evidence: no such statement in the spec or in any source available this session

findings.claim: “Drawing the PLC curve is not a tested exam skill” and, of the Boston Matrix, “Drawing it is not a tested exam skill”
findings.truth: The spec gives no drawing exemption for the product life cycle or the Boston Matrix. Where AQA means it, it says so explicitly: “Students will not be asked to draw or interpret stock control charts” and “Students will not be expected to draw break-even charts”. The absence of the same wording in 3.5.4 makes the claim unsafe advice.
findings.evidence: spec 3.5.4 vs the explicit exemptions at 3.3 (stock control) and 3.6 (break-even)

findings.claim: Section heading “Generic Answers Cap at ~4/6”; “Examiners are explicit about this: an answer that just describes ‘TV adverts reach lots of people’ … caps out at about 4 marks on a 6-mark question”; the same cap in the exam tip and in practice question 5’s mark scheme
findings.truth: There is no published 4-out-of-6 cap and AQA has not said this. Application does gate the top band, so the advice can be kept without the invented number and without the appeal to examiners.
findings.evidence: spec section 4 (assessment objectives); no such rule in the spec

findings.claim: “Aviva sponsoring the Premiership Rugby league” given in the present tense
findings.truth: Aviva’s title sponsorship of English rugby union’s Premiership ran 2010–2018. Arthur J. Gallagher has held it since 2018 (Gallagher Premiership, rebranded Gallagher PREM in 2025).

findings.claim: “Primark … refuses to sell online”, repeated as “no online sale” and “hugely profitable without any online sales” in two mark schemes and in flashcard 10
findings.truth: Primark launched an online click-and-collect service in November 2022 and has since extended it across its UK stores. It still offers no home delivery, which is the point the lesson actually needs.

findings.claim: “A balanced answer with a named UK business for each side will reach the top band.”
findings.truth: Balance plus application is not enough on a 12-mark evaluate question; the top band also needs a clear, justified conclusion.
findings.evidence: spec section 4 (AO3 evaluation: make judgements and draw conclusions)

findings.claim: practice question 5 mark scheme ends “[6 marks — generic answers cap around 4]”
ASOS is “reaching customers in over 200 countries”
findings.truth: There are about 195 countries, so the figure is impossible. ASOS reports selling into roughly 200 markets.
findings.evidence: arithmetic against the UN member-state count

summary: Fourteen findings across five of the six lessons: one HIGH (niche marketing defined as differentiated marketing, in both the glossary and the in-text definition), ten MEDIUM and three LOW; thirteen are FIX and one is a NOTE, giving 22 edits. Every practice tariff is a real AQA tariff (1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 12) with no paper, section or SPaG claim anywhere in the unit, and every Boston Matrix quadrant, life-cycle stage, pricing definition, knowledge-check key, match-question order and calculation was recomputed and is correct. The damage is a cluster of fabricated examiner and mark-scheme claims (an invented 4-out-of-6 cap, two straight-into-the-top-band rules, two not-a-tested-exam-skill claims) plus four dated UK examples (Topshop, Wispa, Aviva, Primark).
